articleTitle: Experience in the use of electrical discharges for the treatment of dusts arising in the steel industry
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Destruction of Waste and Toxic Materials Using Electric Discharges
abstract: The author describes how British Steel Stainless operates a viable process for the recovery of high value metallic wastes from dust generated by the electric arc stainless steelmaking process. The process uses a high power electrical discharge as the prime energy source. IT has not proved practicable to use plasma torches for this application, as their life is severely impaired and their energy transfer mechanisms are not suited to the process. Substantial benefits have accrued by replacing the plasma torches with carbon arcs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The thermal treatment of chemical wastes in plasma processes
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Destruction of Waste and Toxic Materials Using Electric Discharges
abstract: Several advantages are claimed for the application of plasma technology to the high temperature treatment of materials. In particular, plasma systems may be compact, may operate with a high degree of independence of the chemical and physical nature of the input materials and of the intended chemistry of the process, and respond very rapidly to control. The perceived demand for the safe disposal of waste materials has encouraged examination of the application of plasma technology to the problem, particularly for the most hazardous wastes generated by industry. Here, some early results are described of work in which model chemicals simulating some of the more difficult waste compositions, were injected into a 50kW experimental plasma system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Thermal and non-thermal electric discharge processes for chemical synthesis in waste destruction
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Destruction of Waste and Toxic Materials Using Electric Discharges
abstract: Electric discharges can be used for the synthesis or destruction of chemical compounds. Potential advantages include higher temperature and energy densities than combustion processes, alternative chemical routes and greater conversion efficiencies where selective chemical transitions can be carried out. The application of this technique to waste destruction methods is described by the author.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High temperature incineration of hazardous wastes-today's best available technology
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Destruction of Waste and Toxic Materials Using Electric Discharges
abstract: Waste disposal practices and procedures are being very much driven by legislation and greater public awareness of environmental issues. This factor and the enhanced desire to 'destroy', as opposed to 'dump' provides opportunities for higher technology solutions. High temperature incineration is such a solution is generally acknowledged worldwide as the best available technology for the destruction of hazardous and toxic waste in whatever physical form. Here, the author presents an overview of this subject as a benchmark for assessment and comparison of the capabilities and performance of alternative and/or developing technologies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: UK opportunities for plasma applications arising from environmental legislation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Destruction of Waste and Toxic Materials Using Electric Discharges
abstract: The author looks at some important environmental legislation, its change implications for UK industrial manufacturing and waste management, identifies where the main environmental plasma opportunities will lie, and discusses how they could be better exploited. This work is based on recent and on-going projects in materials and the environment at the Centre for Exploitation of Science and Technology (CEST), London, UK.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Plasma pyrolysis of hazardous process and biological hospital waste
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Destruction of Waste and Toxic Materials Using Electric Discharges
abstract: The desire to minimise pollution goes hand in hand with the development of new techniques for the efficient treatment of toxic and hazardous wastes. The desire for zero emission processes has led to the testing of plasma systems which have proved to be more efficient than traditional incineration. Here, the author describes how Strathclyde University are interested in the development of small scale, compact stand-alone units intended for use by hospitals, industry and research laboratories for the safe destruction of biological wastes close to their point of production. Details of this system are presented along with other systems under development including those being constructed in France (Electricity de France).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Destruction of waste or toxic gases and vapours in gliding arc reactor
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Destruction of Waste and Toxic Materials Using Electric Discharges
abstract: A new energy efficient plasma reactor based on gliding discharges at atmospheric pressure is described. It can easily process every kind of gas or vapor, either cold or hot. A large ionized gas volume obtained at low energy density gives an out-of-thermal equilibrium and an extremely reactive medium especially adapted to incinerate or decompose waste and toxic gas or vapor. Two trials performed in laboratory and industrial scale reactors proposed for wide ranges of gas flow (up to 5000 m/sup 3//h) and dissipated electric power (up to 250 kW) are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
